claims.claim: Coccidiomorphs is the group containing most medically important apicomplexans.
claims.source: The protococcidian Eleutheroschizon duboscqi was a sister of eucoccidians, and rhytidocystids branched as basal coccidiomorphs, the group containing most medically important apicomplexans.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the coccidiomorph group.

claims.claim: The blastogregarine Siedleckia was strongly related to the archigregarine Selenidium pygospionis.
claims.source: The blastogregarine Siedleckia was strongly related to the archigregarine Selenidium pygospionis.
claims.evidence: This is a phylogenetic relationship determined from the analysis.

claims.claim: Gregarine apicomplexans and eugregarines were both monophyletic, in contrast to most interpretations based on ribosomal RNA genes.
claims.source: Gregarine apicomplexans (sensu lato including blastogregarines but excluding Digyalum; see below) and eugregarines were both monophyletic, in contrast to most interpretations based on ribosomal RNA genes (rDNA) (Cavalier-Smith, 2014; Leander, 2008; Rueckert et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a phylogenetic finding that contradicts previous hypotheses, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Datasets excluding Cephaloidophora and Gregarina produced trees with congruent topologies.
claims.source: To test relationships between major apicomplexan lineages, we analyzed datasets in which the two longest branches in the tree, Cephaloidophora and Gregarina, were excluded either individually or both together (LG+C60+F+G4+PMSF model with UFBoot2 supports). The resulting trees had congruent topologies with all internal branches fully supported except for two eugregarine subclades and the position of cryptosporidians (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes a robustness test of the phylogenetic results.

claims.claim: Seven statistical tests on 105 tree topologies rejected all alternative topologies at p=0.01 except those differing in the placement of cryptosporidians.
claims.source: Similarly, seven statistical tests on 105 tree topologies representing all possible relationships between coccidiomorphs, cryptosporidians, eugregarines, archigregarines, and blastogregarines rejected all alternative topologies at p=0.01 except those differing in the placement of cryptosporidians (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This describes statistical tests supporting the phylogenetic results.

claims.claim: The relationship of cryptosporidians requires additional support.
claims.source: The relationship of cryptosporidians therefore requires additional support, although their sister position to gregarines, which was unambiguously recovered in all trees including the ten PhyloBayes runs, is a preferred hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the uncertainty in the phylogenetic position of cryptosporidians.

claims.claim: The sister position of cryptosporidians to gregarines is a preferred hypothesis.
claims.source: The relationship of cryptosporidians therefore requires additional support, although their sister position to gregarines, which was unambiguously recovered in all trees including the ten PhyloBayes runs, is a preferred hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is based on the consistent recovery of this relationship in phylogenetic analyses.

claims.claim: Digyalum oweni, a formally described archigregarine, was fully resolved as a sister lineage to all apicomplexans and chrompodellids.
claims.source: Digyalum oweni, a formally described archigregarine was fully resolved as a sister lineage to all apicomplexans and chrompodellids.
claims.evidence: This is a phylogenetic relationship determined from the analysis.

claims.claim: A previously undescribed parasitic symbiont of the annelid Scoloplos with apicomplexan-like traits, named 'Symbiont X', was specifically related to Chromera velia.
claims.source: A previously undescribed parasitic symbiont of the annelid Scoloplos with apicomplexan-like traits, named 'Symbiont X', was specifically related to Chromera velia.
claims.evidence: This is a phylogenetic relationship determined from the analysis.

claims.claim: Apicomplexan parasites in the traditional sense are polyphyletic.
claims.source: Thus, apicomplexan parasites in the traditional sense are polyphyletic (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic positions of Digyalum and Symbiont X.

claims.claim: Digyalum, Selenidium, Siedleckia, rhytidocystids, and Eleutheroschizon all contain near-complete plastidial biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids, ferredoxin redox system, iron-sulfur cluster synthesis, and plastid genomes.
claims.source: Digyalum, Selenidium, Siedleckia, rhytidocystids, and Eleutheroschizon all contain near-complete plastidial biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids, ferredoxin redox system, iron-sulfur cluster synthesis, and plastid genomes (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of plastid genes in transcriptomes, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The eugregarine Lankesteria unusually contains fatty acid biosynthesis as the only plastidial pathway.
claims.source: The eugregarine Lankesteria unusually contains fatty acid biosynthesis as the only plastidial pathway, whereas Symbiont X contains only the isoprenoid pathway, similar to piroplasms (Lizundia et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of plastid genes in transcriptomes, with a citation for comparison to piroplasms.

claims.claim: Symbiont X contains only the isoprenoid pathway, similar to piroplasms.
claims.source: The eugregarine Lankesteria unusually contains fatty acid biosynthesis as the only plastidial pathway, whereas Symbiont X contains only the isoprenoid pathway, similar to piroplasms (Lizundia et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of plastid genes in transcriptomes, with a citation for comparison to piroplasms.

claims.claim: Both Lankesteria and Symbiont X appear to lack plastid genomes.
claims.source: Both Lankesteria and Symbiont X appear to lack plastid genomes (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of plastid genome sequences in transcriptomes, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The distribution of control, signature plastid genes involved in polypeptide import, folding, and DNA replication in the plastid (cpn60, sDer-1, PREX), matches the presence of plastid metabolism and genomes.
claims.source: The distribution of control, signature plastid genes involved in polypeptide import, folding, and DNA replication in the plastid (cpn60, sDer-1, PREX), matches the presence of plastid metabolism and genomes (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the gene distribution data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Maximum likelihood phylogenies of all individual proteins allowed distinguishing apicomplexan sequences from bacteria and other contaminants.
claims.source: Maximum likelihood phylogenies of all individual proteins allowed us to readily distinguish the apicomplexan sequences from bacteria and other contaminants in the datasets (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the method used to verify sequence identity.

claims.claim: In most phylogenies, the apicomplexan sequences cluster with algal plastid forms, confirming that they came from the plastid endosymbiont rather than the eukaryotic host.
claims.source: In most phylogenies, the apicomplexan sequences cluster with algal plastid forms, confirming that they came from the plastid endosymbiont rather than the eukaryotic host.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of individual plastid genes.

claims.claim: N-terminal regions of plastid sequences from new transcriptomes often carry signal peptides typical for targeting to the plastid.
claims.source: N-terminal regions of plastid sequences from our new transcriptomes often carry signal peptides typical for targeting to the plastid (the other have incomplete N-termini or lack targeting signatures by default, such as most triose phosphate translocators).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational prediction of signal peptides.

claims.claim: Signal peptides are often followed by transit peptide-like regions, although these are more difficult to predict computationally.
claims.source: The signal peptides are often followed by transit peptide-like regions, although these are more difficult to predict computationally (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational prediction of transit peptides.

claims.claim: In Digyalum, transit peptides have a net positive charge similar to other plastid leaders.
claims.source: In Digyalum, transit peptides have a net positive charge similar to other plastid leaders (they are low in acidic and high in basic residues; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of amino acid composition of transit peptides, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Digyalum transit peptides are compositionally similar to transit peptides in Plasmodium.
claims.source: Digyalum transit peptides are compositionally similar to transit peptides in Plasmodium, and likewise lack the phenylalanine motif at the first position after the signal peptide cleavage site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Patron and Waller, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of transit peptide composition, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, with a citation for comparison.

claims.claim: Digyalum transit peptides lack the phenylalanine motif at the first position after the signal peptide cleavage site.
claims.source: Digyalum transit peptides are compositionally similar to transit peptides in Plasmodium, and likewise lack the phenylalanine motif at the first position after the signal peptide cleavage site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Patron and Waller, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of transit peptide sequences, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, with a citation for comparison.

claims.claim: Predicted localizations for plastidial proteins and mitochondrial ALAS correspond closely to experimental evidence in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
claims.source: Predicted localizations for plastidial proteins and mitochondrial ALAS correspond closely to experimental evidence in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of predicted and experimental localizations, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The last three enzymes in heme biosynthesis are predicted to be plastidial in some parasites.
claims.source: The only exceptions to this pattern are the last three enzymes in heme biosynthesis, which are predicted to be plastidial in some parasites (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein localization.

claims.claim: The reconstructed plastid pathways reflect known dependencies between their modules.
claims.source: The reconstructed plastid pathways also reflect known dependencies between their modules (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of pathway dependencies, as shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Iron-sulphur cluster assembly and ferredoxin system are widely required as co-factors for isoprenoid and fatty acid synthesis.
claims.source: Iron-sulphur cluster assembly and ferredoxin system are widely required as co-factors for isoprenoid and fatty acid synthesis, whereas heme biosynthesis can be lost independently of other modules – likely the case in Lankesteria and Symbiont X.
claims.evidence: This is based on known biochemical dependencies and the observed gene distribution.

claims.claim: Heme biosynthesis can be lost independently of other modules.
claims.source: Iron-sulphur cluster assembly and ferredoxin system are widely required as co-factors for isoprenoid and fatty acid synthesis, whereas heme biosynthesis can be lost independently of other modules – likely the case in Lankesteria and Symbiont X.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed gene distribution in Lankesteria and Symbiont X.

claims.claim: The synthesis of 3-phosphoglycerate (GAPDH-II and PGK-II) is present selectively.
claims.source: The synthesis of 3-phosphoglycerate (GAPDH-II and PGK-II) is present selectively.
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed gene distribution.

claims.claim: SufA was not identified in the Chromera genome.
claims.source: SufA was not identified in the Chromera genome.
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of the gene in the genome.

claims.claim: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and fatty and lipoic acid synthesis protein sequences in Digyalum are notably divergent.
claims.source: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and fatty and lipoic acid synthesis protein sequences in Digyalum are notably divergent, including three that are more closely related to bacterial than plastid sequences (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of these proteins, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Three protein sequences in Digyalum are more closely related to bacterial than plastid sequences.
claims.source: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and fatty and lipoic acid synthesis protein sequences in Digyalum are notably divergent, including three that are more closely related to bacterial than plastid sequences (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of these proteins, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The cytosolic mevalonate pathway for isoprenoid precursor synthesis is absent in all species.
claims.source: The cytosolic mevalonate pathway for isoprenoid precursor synthesis is absent in all species, but the mitochondrial cysteine desulphurase (IscS) and cytosolic fatty acid synthase (FASI) and elongase (ELO) pathways are present, as expected (Materials and methods) (Dellibovi-Ragheb et al., 2013; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of genes for this pathway, with citations for expected pathways.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial cysteine desulphurase (IscS) and cytosolic fatty acid synthase (FASI) and elongase (ELO) pathways are present, as expected.
claims.source: The cytosolic mevalonate pathway for isoprenoid precursor synthesis is absent in all species, but the mitochondrial cysteine desulphurase (IscS) and cytosolic fatty acid synthase (FASI) and elongase (ELO) pathways are present, as expected (Materials and methods) (Dellibovi-Ragheb et al., 2013; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on the presence of genes for these pathways, with citations for expected pathways.

claims.claim: No plastid genes were identified in five eugregarine lineages other than Lankesteria, including in the draft genome of Gregarina.
claims.source: No plastid genes were identified in five eugregarine lineages other than Lankesteria, including in the draft genome of Gregarina (Figure 2A; see Discussion about the PREX fragment in Ascogregarina).
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of plastid genes in transcriptomes and genomes, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: This result is suggestive of at least two losses of plastids in eugregarines, which were independent of the one in Cryptosporidium.
claims.source: This result is suggestive of at least two losses of plastids in eugregarines, which were independent of the one in Cryptosporidium (Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plastid presence/absence.

claims.claim: Ten novel ARLs were discovered among environmental 16S rDNAs in GenBank and clustered 16S rDNAs obtained from the VAMPS database.
claims.source: Here, we discovered ten novel ARLs among environmental 16S rDNAs in GenBank and clustered 16S rDNAs obtained from the VAMPS database (Huse et al., 2014) by a phylogenetic sorting approach similar to the one used previously (Janouškovec et al., 2012) (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the discovery of novel plastid lineages from environmental sequences.

claims.claim: The use of two ARL-X and ARL-XI described recently is discontinued.
claims.source: We also discontinue the use of two ARL-X and ARL-XI described recently (Mathur et al., 2018), which we find to be members of the Vitrella clade (ARL-I; Figure 3A) and bacterial contaminants, respectively (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis showing these are not distinct lineages, as shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: ARL-X is a member of the Vitrella clade (ARL-I).
claims.source: We also discontinue the use of two ARL-X and ARL-XI described recently (Mathur et al., 2018), which we find to be members of the Vitrella clade (ARL-I; Figure 3A) and bacterial contaminants, respectively (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis, as shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: ARL-XI is a bacterial contaminant.
claims.source: We also discontinue the use of two ARL-X and ARL-XI described recently (Mathur et al., 2018), which we find to be members of the Vitrella clade (ARL-I; Figure 3A) and bacterial contaminants, respectively (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis showing it groups with bacteria.

claims.claim: The total number of unidentified ARLs is 15, in addition to three ARLs represented by Chromera, Vitrella, and corallicolid clades.
claims.source: This brings the total number of unidentified ARLs to 15, in addition to three ARLs represented by Chromera, Vitrella, and corallicolid clades (see Supplementary file 6 for reference sequences for all ARLs).
claims.evidence: This is a count of the known and novel ARLs.

claims.claim: Many plastids in apicomplexans and their relatives are yet to be discovered.
claims.source: A global, maximum likelihood phylogeny of 16S rDNAs of bacteria, plastids and ARLs (including representative sequences of known ARLs and all GenBank and VAMPS centroid sequences of novel ARLs) readily illustrates that many plastids in apicomplexans and their relatives are yet to be discovered (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of ARLs in the phylogeny, as shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Some new ARLs (ARL-XV, ARL-XVI, ARL-XVII) are comparatively diversified and abundant.
claims.source: It also shows that some new ARLs (ARL-XV, ARL-XVI, ARL-XVII) are comparatively diversified and abundant.
claims.evidence: This is based on the number and diversity of sequences in these ARLs.

claims.claim: None of the ARLs corresponds to the plastid 16S rDNAs of Digyalum, Eleutheroschizon, Siedleckia, Selenidium or Rhytidocystis.
claims.source: Despite that ARLs have now more than doubled in number, none of them corresponds to the plastid 16S rDNAs of Digyalum, Eleutheroschizon, Siedleckia, Selenidium or Rhytidocystis.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of 16S rDNA sequences.

claims.claim: The five genera have some of the fastest-evolving and most AT-rich 16S rDNAs of all apicomplexans.
claims.source: Instead, the five genera have some of the fastest-evolving and most AT-rich 16S rDNAs of all apicomplexans, and they cluster with compositionally similar sequences of the more distantly related hematozoans (compare Figure 1A and Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of 16S rDNA sequences, as shown in Figures 1A and 3A.

claims.claim: The five genera cluster with compositionally similar sequences of the more distantly related hematozoans.
claims.source: Instead, the five genera have some of the fastest-evolving and most AT-rich 16S rDNAs of all apicomplexans, and they cluster with compositionally similar sequences of the more distantly related hematozoans (compare Figure 1A and Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of 16S rDNA sequences, as shown in Figures 1A and 3A.

claims.claim: Such artificial grouping of highly divergent sequences is a well-known phylogenetic artifact.
claims.source: Such artificial grouping of highly divergent sequences is a well-known phylogenetic artifact, and deep-level relationships in the tree thus ought to be interpreted with caution.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about phylogenetic artifacts.

claims.claim: The 16S rDNAs of Digyalum, Eleutheroschizon, Siedleckia, Selenidium or Rhytidocystis were recovered among a set of AT-rich transcriptomic contigs, which encode other genes typical of apicomplexan plastid genomes.
claims.source: The 16S rDNAs of Digyalum, Eleutheroschizon, Siedleckia, Selenidium or Rhytidocystis were recovered among a set of AT-rich transcriptomic contigs, which encode other genes typical of apicomplexan plastid genomes (Supplementary file 7; Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the identification of plastid genomes in transcriptomes.

claims.claim: In Rhytidocystis species 1 and 2, the AT content of 16S rDNAs (84% and 86%, respectively) and plastidial transcripts (88% and 91%, respectively) is among the highest of all plastid genomes described to date.
claims.source: In Rhytidocystis species 1 and 2, the AT content of 16S rDNAs (84% and 86%, respectively) and plastidial transcripts (88% and 91%, respectively) is among the highest of all plastid genomes described to date (Figure 3B) (Su et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of AT content, as shown in Figure 3B, with a citation for comparison.

claims.claim: Digyalum, Siedleckia, Selenidium, and Rhytidocystis sp. one use a non-canonical genetic code in which UGA encodes for tryptophan.
claims.source: Digyalum, Siedleckia, Selenidium, and Rhytidocystis sp. one use a non-canonical genetic code in which UGA encodes for tryptophan; UGA is absent in the fragmentary plastid DNA of Rhytidocystis sp. two and encodes for STOP codons in Eleutheroschizon (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: UGA is absent in the fragmentary plastid DNA of Rhytidocystis sp. two.
claims.source: Digyalum, Siedleckia, Selenidium, and Rhytidocystis sp. one use a non-canonical genetic code in which UGA encodes for tryptophan; UGA is absent in the fragmentary plastid DNA of Rhytidocystis sp. two and encodes for STOP codons in Eleutheroschizon (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: UGA encodes for STOP codons in Eleutheroschizon.
claims.source: Digyalum, Siedleckia, Selenidium, and Rhytidocystis sp. one use a non-canonical genetic code in which UGA encodes for tryptophan; UGA is absent in the fragmentary plastid DNA of Rhytidocystis sp. two and encodes for STOP codons in Eleutheroschizon (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The Digyalum plastid encodes six genes never identified in apicomplexan plastids.
claims.source: The Digyalum plastid encodes six genes never identified in apicomplexan plastids and lacks nine genes they do contain; only one gene (rps18) was relocated to the nucleus in parallel in both lineages (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid genome contents, as shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The Digyalum plastid lacks nine genes that apicomplexan plastids contain.
claims.source: The Digyalum plastid encodes six genes never identified in apicomplexan plastids and lacks nine genes they do contain; only one gene (rps18) was relocated to the nucleus in parallel in both lineages (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid genome contents, as shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Only one gene (rps18) was relocated to the nucleus in parallel in both Digyalum and apicomplexan lineages.
claims.source: The Digyalum plastid encodes six genes never identified in apicomplexan plastids and lacks nine genes they do contain; only one gene (rps18) was relocated to the nucleus in parallel in both lineages (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid genome contents, as shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The unusual plastid DNA replication and repair complex (PREX) is found in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum.
claims.source: To test if the plastids in Digyalum, chrompodellids and apicomplexans are likely derived from a common source we searched for shared innovations in their plastid genes. We observed that the unusual plastid DNA replication and repair complex (PREX) (Seow et al., 2005) is found not only in apicomplexans and chrompodellids (Janouškovec et al., 2015) but also in Digyalum (Figure 2A and Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of PREX in transcriptomes, as shown in Figures 2A and 4, with citations.

claims.claim: PREX protein contains N-terminal primase and helicase domains, which are homologous to the mitochondrial primase-helicase Twinkle and fused with an Aquifex-type exonuclease-polymerase downstream.
claims.source: PREX protein contains N-terminal primase and helicase domains, which are homologous to the mitochondrial primase-helicase Twinkle and fused with an Aquifex-type exonuclease-polymerase downstream.
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the PREX protein.

claims.claim: Phylogeny of the polymerase unit confirms that it was acquired from an unknown bacterial source related to Aquifex before the Digyalum-apicomplexan split.
claims.source: Phylogeny of the polymerase unit confirms that it was acquired from an unknown bacterial source related to Aquifex before the Digyalum-apicomplexan split (Figure 4A,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the polymerase domain, as shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claims.claim: The PREX gene subsequently fused with the Twinkle gene and the product became targeted to the plastid.
claims.source: The gene subsequently fused with the Twinkle gene and the product became targeted to the plastid (the N-terminus of PREX is incomplete in most species including Digyalum but contains a signal peptide in Chromera; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structure of the PREX protein and the presence of signal peptides.

claims.claim: A canonical plastid ispH gene of a cyanobacterial origin, which is also present in dinoflagellates and Perkinsus, was replaced by a Chlamydiae-like variant in the ancestor of Digyalum and Apicomplexa.
claims.source: A canonical plastid ispH gene of a cyanobacterial origin, which is also present in dinoflagellates and Perkinsus, was replaced by a Chlamydiae-like variant in the ancestor of Digyalum and Apicomplexa and fused with the plastid gene for sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase form 3 (SBP3) (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of ispH, as shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: The Chlamydiae-like ispH variant fused with the plastid gene for sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase form 3 (SBP3).
claims.source: A canonical plastid ispH gene of a cyanobacterial origin, which is also present in dinoflagellates and Perkinsus, was replaced by a Chlamydiae-like variant in the ancestor of Digyalum and Apicomplexa and fused with the plastid gene for sedoheptulose-1,7-bisphosphatase form 3 (SBP3) (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of gene structure, as shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: The ispH-SBP3 fusion is absent in Toxoplasma, Plasmodium and piroplasms, which lack SBP3.
claims.source: The fusion is absent in Toxoplasma, Plasmodium and piroplasms, which lack SBP3, and has been interpreted as a derived characteristic in Chromera (Petersen et al., 2014), but instead we find it is broadly distributed in apicomplexans and their relatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed gene distribution, with a citation for previous interpretation.

claims.claim: The ispH-SBP3 fusion has been interpreted as a derived characteristic in Chromera, but is instead broadly distributed in apicomplexans and their relatives.
claims.source: The fusion is absent in Toxoplasma, Plasmodium and piroplasms, which lack SBP3, and has been interpreted as a derived characteristic in Chromera (Petersen et al., 2014), but instead we find it is broadly distributed in apicomplexans and their relatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed gene distribution, with a citation for previous interpretation.

claims.claim: Another unique evolutionary event in apicomplexan plastids is a fission in a non-conserved region of the plastid-encoded rpoC2 gene.
claims.source: Another unique evolutionary event in apicomplexan plastids is a fission in a non-conserved region of the plastid-encoded rpoC2 gene.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome structure.

claims.claim: The unprecedented split in rpoC2 was once interpreted as a read-through frame shift (in Plasmodium) or read-through STOP codons (in Toxoplasma and Eimeria) in a continuous rpoC2.
claims.source: The unprecedented split was once interpreted as a read-through frame shift (in Plasmodium) or read-through STOP codons (in Toxoplasma and Eimeria) in a continuous rpoC2 (Cai et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous interpretations.

claims.claim: All apicomplexan rpoC2 genes are split within the same region, including those in the deep-branching Selenidium and Siedleckia.
claims.source: We instead find that all apicomplexan rpoC2 genes are split within the same region, including those in the deep-branching Selenidium and Siedleckia (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The two rpoC2 moieties are found in different reading frames in most species.
claims.source: The two rpoC2 moieties are found in different reading frames in most species, but two different in-frame STOP codons (UAA and UAG) separate them in Toxoplasma.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences.

claims.claim: Two different in-frame STOP codons (UAA and UAG) separate the two rpoC2 moieties in Toxoplasma.
claims.source: The two rpoC2 moieties are found in different reading frames in most species, but two different in-frame STOP codons (UAA and UAG) separate them in Toxoplasma.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences.

claims.claim: Both frame shifting and STOP codon read-through would be required for continuous rpoC2 translation in Eleutheroschizon.
claims.source: Both frame shifting and STOP codon read-through would be required for continuous rpoC2 translation in Eleutheroschizon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Such variable gene arrangements are incongruent with the expression of the apicomplexan rpoC2 as a single protein.
claims.source: Such variable gene arrangements are incongruent with the expression of the apicomplexan rpoC2 as a single protein.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene structure.

claims.claim: Messenger RNA editing does not correct the rpoC2 reading frame in Plasmodium.
claims.source: Messenger RNA editing likewise does not correct the rpoC2 reading frame in Plasmodium (Nisbet et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on RNA editing.

claims.claim: The downstream rpoC2 moiety almost unequivocally possesses an ATG start codon near the split site allowing it to be translated independently.

claims.claim: The evidence points to a fission event in rpoC2, which is absent in all other plastids, including those of Digyalum and chrompodellids.

claims.claim: The rpoC2 fission represents a defining ancestral characteristic of the apicomplexan plastid.

claims.claim: Alphaproteobacteria-like ferrochelatase (HemH) is localized to mitochondria in Plasmodium but likely targeted to plastids in Chromera and possibly in some apicomplexans.

claims.claim: Verrucomicrobia-like beta-ketoacyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabG) is present in apicomplexan and chrompodellid plastids.
claims.source: The first is Alphaproteobacteria-like ferrochelatase (HemH), which is localized to mitochondria in Plasmodium but likely targeted to plastids in Chromera and possibly in some apicomplexans (see Discussion) (Koreny et al., 2011; Sato and Wilson, 2003; Varadharajan et al., 2004), and the other is Verrucomicrobia-like beta-ketoacyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabG) (Janouškovec et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Digyalum encodes the same alphaproteobacterial HemH but it has an unusual FabG, which is related to other bacteria.
claims.source: Digyalum encodes the same alphaproteobacterial HemH but it has an unusual FabG, which is related to other bacteria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of these proteins, as shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Genes of two well-known cytosolic proteins (lactate/malate dehydrogenase and glutamine synthase type I) were acquired from bacteria in the Digyalum-Apicomplexa ancestor.

claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of these proteins, as shown in Figure 4C, with citations.

claims.claim: Two species with apicomplexan-like morphology either described as apicomplexans (Digyalum) or yet unclassified (Symbiont X) are not members of Apicomplexa sensu stricto.
claims.source: Two species with apicomplexan-like morphology either described as apicomplexans (Digyalum) or yet unclassified (Symbiont X) are not members of Apicomplexa sensu stricto.
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic positions of these species.

claims.claim: Apicomplexan-like parasites evolved at least three times independently.
claims.source: This shows that apicomplexan-like parasites are polyphyletic and evolved at least three times independently.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic positions of Digyalum, Symbiont X, and Apicomplexa sensu stricto.

claims.claim: Large trophont stages attached to intestines of marine invertebrates by specialized apical structures are products of convergent evolution.
claims.source: Specifically, large trophont stages attached to intestines of marine invertebrates by specialized apical structures are products of convergent evolution.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the polyphyletic nature of parasites with these characteristics.

claims.claim: The trophonts of Digyalum parasitize the gut epithelium of Littorina snails and their attachment structure contains an apical complex with a protruded polar ring, which provides a gateway for rhoptry-mediated secretion.
claims.source: The trophonts of Digyalum, for example, parasitize the gut epithelium of Littorina snails and their attachment structure contains an apical complex with a protruded polar ring, which provides a gateway for rhoptry-mediated secretion – a combination of traits typical for gregarine apicomplexans (Dyson et al., 1994; Dyson et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Digyalum morphology.

claims.claim: Symbiont X parasitizes the gut of Scoloplos armiger polychaetes being attached to the host epithelium by its apical end.
claims.source: Symbiont X is known only from light microscopy data but would be also readily classified as an apicomplexan based on crude characteristics: it parasitizes the gut of Scoloplos armiger polychaetes being attached to the host epithelium by its apical end (unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is based on unpublished observations.

claims.claim: Apical complexes with rhoptries, micronemes and pseudoconoids are present in free-living relatives of apicomplexans, such as in the predatory Colpodella and Psammosa and photosynthetic Chromera, and in more distantly related parasites such as Perkinsus and Parvilucifera.
claims.source: Apical complexes with rhoptries, micronemes and pseudoconoids are present in free-living relatives of apicomplexans, such as in the predatory Colpodella and Psammosa and photosynthetic Chromera, and in more distantly related parasites such as Perkinsus and Parvilucifera (Foissner and Foissner, 1984; Norén et al., 1999; Oborník et al., 2011; Okamoto and Keeling, 2014; Perkins, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on these organisms.

claims.claim: The broad distribution of apical complexes points to a single origin of the apical complex in the ancestor of apicomplexans and dinoflagellates in a non-parasitic context.
claims.source: Such broad distribution points to a single origin of the apical complex in the ancestor of apicomplexans and dinoflagellates in a non-parasitic context (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of the apical complex, as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The apical complex is likely an important precondition in multiple origins of parasitism in both apicomplexans and dinoflagellates.
claims.source: Because the apical complex mediates secretion often associated with cell-to-cell interactions, it is likely an important precondition in multiple origins of parasitism in both apicomplexans and dinoflagellates.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the function of the apical complex and its distribution.

claims.claim: The use of the apical complex in extracellular attachment and secretion in the gut epithelium of animal hosts may have triggered convergent expansion in the cell size of gregarine, Digyalum and Symbiont X trophonts.
claims.source: In similar host environments the structure may have also promoted convergent parasite morphologies. The use of the apical complex in extracellular attachment and secretion in the gut epithelium of animal hosts, for example, may have triggered convergent expansion in the cell size of gregarine, Digyalum and Symbiont X trophonts.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about the role of the apical complex in convergent evolution.

claims.claim: Convergent similarities in Digyalum, Symbiont X, and gregarines are accompanied by considerable differences in detailed morphology.
claims.source: Unsurprisingly, convergent similarities in the three lineages are accompanied by considerable differences in detailed morphology: Digyalum and Symbiont X do not glide or twist but they pulsate, and detailed ultrastructure of their apical complex and pellicle (Dyson et al., 1994; Dyson et al., 1993) (unpublished data) is distinct from that in gregarines (Kováčiková et al., 2017; Paskerova et al., 2018; Valigurová et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on morphology.

claims.claim: Digyalum and Symbiont X do not glide or twist but they pulsate.
claims.source: Unsurprisingly, convergent similarities in the three lineages are accompanied by considerable differences in detailed morphology: Digyalum and Symbiont X do not glide or twist but they pulsate, and detailed ultrastructure of their apical complex and pellicle (Dyson et al., 1994; Dyson et al., 1993) (unpublished data) is distinct from that in gregarines (Kováčiková et al., 2017; Paskerova et al., 2018; Valigurová et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations of motility.

claims.claim: Apicomplexans are well-known auxotrophs for purines, but Digyalum contains a pathway for their synthesis.
claims.source: Similar divergence characterizes their molecular make-ups: apicomplexans are well-known auxotrophs for purines, but Digyalum contains a pathway for their synthesis (data not shown) and, despite that both lineages lost photosynthesis, their plastid genomes have been reduced in different ways (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of purine synthesis genes in Digyalum, as shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Despite that both Digyalum and apicomplexan lineages lost photosynthesis, their plastid genomes have been reduced in different ways.
claims.source: Similar divergence characterizes their molecular make-ups: apicomplexans are well-known auxotrophs for purines, but Digyalum contains a pathway for their synthesis (data not shown) and, despite that both lineages lost photosynthesis, their plastid genomes have been reduced in different ways (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid genome contents, as shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The convergent morphologies of Digyalum, Symbiont X and apicomplexans are superficial similarities.
claims.source: The convergent morphologies of Digyalum, Symbiont X and apicomplexans are therefore rather superficial similarities, but the possibility that they were driven by the presence of shared ancestral traits (such as the apical complex) in similar host habitats highlights the importance of preconditions in the origin of parasites (Janouskovec and Keeling, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in detailed morphology and molecular make-up, with a citation.

claims.claim: The possibility that convergent morphologies were driven by the presence of shared ancestral traits (such as the apical complex) in similar host habitats highlights the importance of preconditions in the origin of parasites.
claims.source: The convergent morphologies of Digyalum, Symbiont X and apicomplexans are therefore rather superficial similarities, but the possibility that they were driven by the presence of shared ancestral traits (such as the apical complex) in similar host habitats highlights the importance of preconditions in the origin of parasites (Janouskovec and Keeling, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference about the role of preconditions in the origin of parasites, with a citation.

claims.claim: Eugregarines and gregarines are unequivocally monophyletic.
claims.source: Key findings of multiprotein phylogenies are that eugregarines and gregarines are unequivocally monophyletic (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The monophyly of eugregarines and gregarines broadly supports traditional morphological classifications.
claims.source: This broadly supports traditional morphological classifications (Grassé, 1953) in contrast to many recent proposals based on rDNA phylogenies, which regard both groups as polyphyletic (Cavalier-Smith, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to traditional classifications and recent proposals.

claims.claim: Many recent proposals based on rDNA phylogenies regard eugregarines and gregarines as polyphyletic.
claims.source: This broadly supports traditional morphological classifications (Grassé, 1953) in contrast to many recent proposals based on rDNA phylogenies, which regard both groups as polyphyletic (Cavalier-Smith, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent proposal.

claims.claim: Protein sequences allow for building larger phylogenetic matrices and have more even substitution rates than rDNAs.
claims.source: Indeed, protein sequences allow for building larger phylogenetic matrices and have more even substitution rates than rDNAs, some of which are notoriously divergent and phylogenetically unstable.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the advantages of protein sequences for phylogenetics.

claims.claim: Some rDNAs are notoriously divergent and phylogenetically unstable.
claims.source: Indeed, protein sequences allow for building larger phylogenetic matrices and have more even substitution rates than rDNAs, some of which are notoriously divergent and phylogenetically unstable.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of rDNA sequences for phylogenetics.

claims.claim: The phylogeny contains six of the seven main eugregarine lineages at the superfamily level.
claims.source: Although the sampling of eugregarine diversity is incomplete, our phylogeny contains six of their seven main lineages at the superfamily level (Simdyanov et al., 2017) – one of them being Polyrhabdina, which is apparently not a lecudinoid (Figure 1A and unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This describes the taxonomic sampling in the phylogeny, as shown in Figure 1A, with a citation.

claims.claim: Polyrhabdina is apparently not a lecudinoid.
claims.source: Although the sampling of eugregarine diversity is incomplete, our phylogeny contains six of their seven main lineages at the superfamily level (Simdyanov et al., 2017) – one of them being Polyrhabdina, which is apparently not a lecudinoid (Figure 1A and unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis, as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The eugregarine monophyly provides the first unambiguous phylogenetic support for their two candidate synapomorphies: the ultrastructure of the epimerite, and the ultrastructure of epicytic crests.
claims.source: The eugregarine monophyly provides the first unambiguous phylogenetic support for their two candidate synapomorphies: the ultrastructure of the epimerite, and the ultrastructure of epicytic crests (Simdyanov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic result, with a citation.

claims.claim: The eugregarine monophyly partially resolves the little understood relationships between eugregarine superfamilies.
claims.source: It also partially resolves the little understood relationships between eugregarine superfamilies (Cavalier-Smith, 2014; Simdyanov et al., 2017; Simdyanov et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic result, with citations.

claims.claim: The blastogregarine Siedleckia groups strongly with the archigregarine Selenidium.
claims.source: The blastogregarine Siedleckia groups strongly with the archigregarine Selenidium.
claims.evidence: This is a phylogenetic relationship determined from the analysis.

claims.claim: Blastogregarines and archigregarines share a combination of characteristics that are rare or absent in other apicomplexans, namely active bending and twisting movement in trophozoites, pellicular folds running along the body length in many species, and one or more layers of longitudinal microtubules underlying the pellicle.
claims.source: The sampling of both groups is incomplete, especially in the archigregarines, but they do share a combination of characteristics that are rare or absent in other apicomplexans, namely active bending and twisting movement in trophozoites, pellicular folds running along the body length in many species, and one or more layers of longitudinal microtubules underlying the pellicle (Schrével et al., 2016; Simdyanov et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on morphology.

claims.claim: Both blastogregarines and archigregarines feed by myzocytosis.
claims.source: Both lineages also feed by myzocytosis, which is known in some relatives of apicomplexans (Foissner and Foissner, 1984; Mylnikov and Mylnikova, 2008) but not in eugregarines, cryptosporidians or coccidiomorphs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on feeding mechanisms.

claims.claim: Myzocytosis is known in some relatives of apicomplexans but not in eugregarines, cryptosporidians or coccidiomorphs.
claims.source: Both lineages also feed by myzocytosis, which is known in some relatives of apicomplexans (Foissner and Foissner, 1984; Mylnikov and Mylnikova, 2008) but not in eugregarines, cryptosporidians or coccidiomorphs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on feeding mechanisms.

claims.claim: The blastogregarine ultrastructure and life cycle share additional similarities with coccidians.
claims.source: Because the blastogregarine ultrastructure and life cycle share additional similarities with coccidians (Simdyanov et al., 2018), confirming their phylogenetic position is important for reconstructing character evolution in Apicomplexa as a whole.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on blastogregarine biology.

claims.claim: Confirming the phylogenetic position of blastogregarines is important for reconstructing character evolution in Apicomplexa as a whole.
claims.source: Because the blastogregarine ultrastructure and life cycle share additional similarities with coccidians (Simdyanov et al., 2018), confirming their phylogenetic position is important for reconstructing character evolution in Apicomplexa as a whole.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the importance of the phylogenetic result.

claims.claim: The monophyly of gregarines sensu lato provides phylogenetic support for a tentative synapomorphy of this group, the forming of a gametocyst during the life cycle.
claims.source: The monophyly of gregarines sensu lato in our trees (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) provides phylogenetic support for a tentative synapomorphy of this group, the forming of a gametocyst during the life cycle (Simdyanov et al., 2017), although this characteristic is absent in blastogregarines.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic result, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, with a citation.

claims.claim: The forming of a gametocyst during the life cycle is absent in blastogregarines.
claims.source: The monophyly of gregarines sensu lato in our trees (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) provides phylogenetic support for a tentative synapomorphy of this group, the forming of a gametocyst during the life cycle (Simdyanov et al., 2017), although this characteristic is absent in blastogregarines.
claims.evidence: This is a known characteristic of blastogregarines.

claims.claim: The position of cryptosporidians is still not fully resolved, but the group is consistently recovered next to gregarines.
claims.source: The position of cryptosporidians is still not fully resolved, but the group is consistently recovered next to gregarines (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Eleutheroschizon is clearly important to understanding the origin of eucoccidians.
claims.source: Eleutheroschizon is clearly important to understanding the origin of eucoccidians (Figure 1A) (Valigurová et al., 2015), although its classification as a protococcidian is apparently incorrect (unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of Eleutheroschizon, as shown in Figure 1A, with a citation.

claims.claim: The classification of Eleutheroschizon as a protococcidian is apparently incorrect.
claims.source: Eleutheroschizon is clearly important to understanding the origin of eucoccidians (Figure 1A) (Valigurová et al., 2015), although its classification as a protococcidian is apparently incorrect (unpublished data).
claims.evidence: This is based on unpublished data.

claims.claim: Two Rhytidocystis species are positioned as a basal group in the class Coccidiomorpha.
claims.source: Two Rhytidocystis species are positioned as a basal group in the class Coccidiomorpha (Figure 1A), which supports traditional views on their classification closer to coccidians (Levine, 1979; Porchet Hennere, 1972) rather than to gregarines (Cavalier-Smith, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis, as shown in Figure 1A, with citations to traditional and recent classifications.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic position of Rhytidocystis supports traditional views on their classification closer to coccidians rather than to gregarines.
claims.source: Two Rhytidocystis species are positioned as a basal group in the class Coccidiomorpha (Figure 1A), which supports traditional views on their classification closer to coccidians (Levine, 1979; Porchet Hennere, 1972) rather than to gregarines (Cavalier-Smith, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic result, as shown in Figure 1A, with citations.

claims.claim: The bigger group that includes rhytidocystids and related parasites of annelids and molluscs provides a stepping stone for understanding the evolution of coccidiomorphs, including the majority of medically important apicomplexans.
claims.source: The bigger group that includes rhytidocystids and related parasites of annelids and molluscs (Kristmundsson et al., 2011) therefore provides a stepping stone for understanding the evolution of coccidiomorphs, including the majority of medically important apicomplexans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the importance of this group for understanding evolution, with a citation.

claims.claim: Plastids are common in deep-branching apicomplexans, despite not having been previously recognized.
claims.source: Evidence for endosymbiotic genes with plastid targeting signals and plastid genomes shows that plastids are common in deep-branching apicomplexans, despite not having been previously recognized (Figure 2, Figure 3 and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on the identification of plastid genes and genomes, as shown in Figures 2 and 3 and Supplementary file 5.

claims.claim: Plastid metabolic networks in deep-branching apicomplexans are similar to those in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium.
claims.source: Their plastid metabolic networks are similar to those in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium and generally serve to produce three essential metabolites: isoprenoid precursors for the synthesis of carotenoids, ubiquinone and prenyls; heme as a protein co-factor; and fatty acids as constituents of cellular lipids (Imlay and Odom, 2014; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; van Dooren et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid pathways, with citations.

claims.claim: Plastid metabolic networks generally serve to produce three essential metabolites: isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids.
claims.source: Their plastid metabolic networks are similar to those in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium and generally serve to produce three essential metabolites: isoprenoid precursors for the synthesis of carotenoids, ubiquinone and prenyls; heme as a protein co-factor; and fatty acids as constituents of cellular lipids (Imlay and Odom, 2014; Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; van Dooren et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plastid metabolism.

claims.claim: Heme biosynthesis is partially localized in the cytosol and mitochondria.
claims.source: Heme biosynthesis is partially localized in the cytosol and mitochondria, and fatty acids can be extended by non-plastidial elongases (Figure 2A) (Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2004), but de novo biosynthesis of all three metabolites outside of the plastid appears to be absent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on heme biosynthesis, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Fatty acids can be extended by non-plastidial elongases.
claims.source: Heme biosynthesis is partially localized in the cytosol and mitochondria, and fatty acids can be extended by non-plastidial elongases (Figure 2A) (Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2004), but de novo biosynthesis of all three metabolites outside of the plastid appears to be absent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fatty acid metabolism, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: De novo biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids outside of the plastid appears to be absent.
claims.source: Heme biosynthesis is partially localized in the cytosol and mitochondria, and fatty acids can be extended by non-plastidial elongases (Figure 2A) (Ramakrishnan et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2004), but de novo biosynthesis of all three metabolites outside of the plastid appears to be absent.
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of genes for these pathways outside the plastid.

claims.claim: The absence of de novo biosynthesis outside the plastid creates dependence on the plastid for the production of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids.
claims.source: This creates dependence on the plastid for the production of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids, which can be overcome only by metabolite uptake from the environment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic capabilities of the plastid.

claims.claim: Dependence on the plastid can be overcome only by metabolite uptake from the environment.
claims.source: This creates dependence on the plastid for the production of isoprenoid precursors, heme, and fatty acids, which can be overcome only by metabolite uptake from the environment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic capabilities of the plastid.

claims.claim: Salvage of host isoprenoids, heme, and fatty acids is common in parasites.
claims.source: Salvage of host isoprenoids, heme, and fatty acids is common in parasites, but obtaining them in sufficient amounts across the life cycle is apparently challenging.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about parasite metabolism.

claims.claim: Obtaining isoprenoids, heme, and fatty acids from the host in sufficient amounts across the life cycle is apparently challenging.
claims.source: Salvage of host isoprenoids, heme, and fatty acids is common in parasites, but obtaining them in sufficient amounts across the life cycle is apparently challenging.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the challenges of metabolite salvage.

claims.claim: Most parasites retain all three plastidial pathways.
claims.source: Most parasites retain all three plastidial pathways, and only two lineages have lost plastid organelles altogether (Figure 5): cryptosporidians (Abrahamsen et al., 2004), and the dinoflagellates Hematodinium and Amoebophrya (Gornik et al., 2015; John et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed distribution of plastid pathways, as shown in Figure 5, with citations.

claims.claim: Only two lineages have lost plastid organelles altogether: cryptosporidians, and the dinoflagellates Hematodinium and Amoebophrya.
claims.source: Most parasites retain all three plastidial pathways, and only two lineages have lost plastid organelles altogether (Figure 5): cryptosporidians (Abrahamsen et al., 2004), and the dinoflagellates Hematodinium and Amoebophrya (Gornik et al., 2015; John et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed distribution of plastid pathways, as shown in Figure 5, with citations.

claims.claim: In free-living organisms, plastids are always retained, perhaps because replacing their metabolism by salvage is even more difficult.
claims.source: In free-living organisms, plastids are always retained, perhaps because replacing their metabolism by salvage is even more difficult (Janouškovec et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about plastid retention in free-living organisms, with a citation.

claims.claim: The biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors is the most consistently required plastidial pathway.
claims.source: Most consistently required is the biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors (Figure 5), which is the only indispensable plastidial pathway in piroplasms, the Plasmodium blood stage, and possibly in Symbiont X (Figure 2A) (Lizundia et al., 2009; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed distribution of plastid pathways, as shown in Figures 2A and 5, with citations.

claims.claim: The biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors is the only indispensable plastidial pathway in piroplasms, the Plasmodium blood stage, and possibly in Symbiont X.
claims.source: Most consistently required is the biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors (Figure 5), which is the only indispensable plastidial pathway in piroplasms, the Plasmodium blood stage, and possibly in Symbiont X (Figure 2A) (Lizundia et al., 2009; Yeh and DeRisi, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed distribution of plastid pathways, as shown in Figures 2A and 5, with citations.

claims.claim: In the eugregarine Lankesteria, fatty acid biosynthesis appears to be the only retained plastidial anabolic pathway.
claims.source: A fully unprecedented situation exists in the eugregarine Lankesteria, where fatty acid biosynthesis appears to be the only retained plastidial anabolic pathway (the transcriptome is fragmentary but enzymes for the biosynthesis of isoprenoid precursors and heme are absent).
claims.evidence: This is based on the observed distribution of plastid pathways in the transcriptome.

claims.claim: The existence of plastids in Selenidium and Rhytidocystis is consistent with ultrastructural reports of multimembrane organelles in some of their species.
claims.source: Interestingly, the existence of plastids in Selenidium and Rhytidocystis is also consistent with ultrastructural reports of multimembrane organelles in some of their species, which correspond to non-photosynthetic plastids in other apicomplexans by size, appearance, and their position near the nucleus (Figure 5) (Leander and Ramey, 2006; Porchet Hennere, 1972; Schrével, 1971; Schrével et al., 2016; Wakeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to ultrastructural studies, as shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Five eugregarines lack any evidence for plastid presence; these include Gregarina where a draft genome is available.
claims.source: Five eugregarines lack any evidence for plastid presence; these include Gregarina where a draft genome is available (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of plastid genes in transcriptomes and genomes, as shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Since Lankesteria is phylogenetically nested among eugregarines lacking plastids, eugregarines must have lost plastids at least twice.
claims.source: Since Lankesteria is phylogenetically nested among them, eugregarines must have lost plastids at least twice (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plastid presence/absence, as shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Ascogregarina contains a fragment of PREX, but because the species lacks evidence for other endosymbiont-derived genes it is conservatively considered to encode for an ex-plastidial protein or is a contaminant.
claims.source: Ascogregarina contains a fragment of PREX (Figure 2A and Figure 4A), but because the species lacks evidence for other endosymbiont-derived genes we conservatively consider it encodes for an ex-plastidial protein or is a contaminant.
